meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Silence is argument carried out by other means'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Che Guevara: the line turns up in Jay Cantor's 1983 novel about him, and quote books pinned it on Che from 1986.

answer.label: Not Che Guevara — traced to a 1983 novel about him
answer.sourceLine: No speech, book or letter by Guevara contains this line. The earliest appearance we found is in the narration of Jay Cantor’s novel The Death of Che Guevara (Knopf, 1983), worded “silence is argument carried on by other means.” Quote books then credited it to Guevara himself, starting with Robert Byrne in 1986.

source.excerpt: The others chattered on for a bit, until they saw him; then, one by one, they too grew quiet; waited. His silence was another manner of argument (silence is argument carried on by other means). When he had said all he could think to say…
source.trailTitle: How a novelist’s sentence became a Che quote
trail: 1983 — The line appears as narration in Jay Cantor’s novel The Death of Che Guevara (Knopf) ↗, catalogued as fiction about Guevara. It is the earliest appearance we found in Internet Archive full-text search ↗.

1986 — Robert Byrne’s The Third and Possibly the Best 637 Best Things Anybody Ever Said ↗ prints it as item 590, credited to “Ernesto ‘Che’ Guevara (1928–1967),” with no source. That is the earliest attribution to Guevara we found.

2005 — Wikiquote’s Che Guevara page ↗ lists the “carried out” version, citing only Earl Ernest Guile’s self-help compilation Secrets to a Richer Life (2005). No speech or writing of Guevara’s is cited.
source.excerptNote: Pieced together from overlapping Internet Archive full-text search snippets of the 1983 Knopf edition and the 1984 Vintage paperback. The scan is lending-restricted, so we did not read the full page. Note the novel says “carried on”; the popular “carried out” is a later drift in quote collections.

author.name: Jay Cantor
author.heading: Who actually wrote it
author.bio: Jay Cantor is an American novelist and essayist who teaches at Tufts University. His first novel, The Death of Che Guevara (Knopf, 1983), is a work of fiction that imagines Guevara’s life and death. Its narration contains the earliest version of this line we could find.

misattribution.heading: Why everyone thinks Che said it
misattribution.intro: The line sounds like a guerrilla’s aphorism: it echoes Clausewitz’s “war is the continuation of politics by other means.” It also turns up in a book with Guevara’s name in the title. Quote compilers took a novelist’s narration for the revolutionary’s own words.

items.why: No source is given in any of the quote collections we found. Even Wikiquote ↗ cites only a 2005 self-help book, not any speech, essay or letter by Guevara.

The line appears, in parentheses, in the narration of Cantor’s 1983 novel The Death of Che Guevara ↗, as “silence is argument carried on by other means.” The book is a work of fiction, so the sentence belongs to Cantor’s narrator, not to Guevara.

Byrne’s 1986 collection The Third and Possibly the Best 637 Best Things Anybody Ever Said ↗ gives it to Guevara with no citation. Byrne’s later omnibus editions and many 1990s–2000s quote books then repeated it.

misattribution.truthLine: Che Guevara did not write or say this. The earliest version we found is Jay Cantor’s, in his 1983 novel The Death of Che Guevara ↗, where it reads “carried on by other means.”

context.heading: A novel’s line gets misread as Guevara’s own
lead: Jay Cantor’s The Death of Che Guevara is a long novel that imagines Guevara’s life and death. In one scene the narrator describes a man whose arrival silences a chattering group, and adds in parentheses: “silence is argument carried on by other means.” Lifted out of the book, the sentence reads like a maxim, and the book’s title supplies a famous name to hang it on.

By 1986 Robert Byrne’s quote anthology was crediting it to Guevara outright. From there it spread through quote dictionaries, textbooks and email signatures. Along the way “carried on” drifted into “carried out,” the wording most sites use today.
detailsBody: “Earliest” here means the earliest we found in the Internet Archive’s full-text search of digitized books. We could not run a matching Google Books search, so an earlier printing can’t be ruled out.
The novel’s copyright page also lists 1977 and 1979, so parts of it may have appeared in print before 1983. We have not checked whether this sentence was in those earlier parts.
Quote Investigator has no article on this quote or on Guevara; searches of its site return nothing.
